title.en: Golden hour dusk with a low warm key

summary: Set a low warm sun against a cool sky fill so long shadows describe the ground and every vertical picks up a rim.
objective: Shadows are several times longer than their casters and run parallel, and the shaded side of each object is cool rather than black.
intent_signals: the scene looks like flat noon
example_prompts: Light a village exterior twenty minutes before sunset.
Give a terrain model long raking shadows that describe its relief.
Warm a street scene without losing detail on the shaded side.
negative_signals: quantitative solar position for a date and latitude
not_for: Interiors lit by controlled fixtures rather than by the sky.
Scenes that must state a real solar elevation for a date and latitude, which needs a sourced solar model.

principles: A low sun is a shape tool. At 6 deg elevation shadows run several times the height of their casters, and those shadows describe the ground plane better than any texture.
The warmth must be paid for with a cool counterpart. A warm key alone reads as an orange filter; a warm key against a blue sky fill reads as time of day.
The sun disc is the brightest thing in frame and everything else is graded relative to it, which is why exposure sits below 1 rather than the key being lowered.
Fog colour belongs to the horizon band, not to the zenith. Matching it makes distance dissolve into the sunset instead of into haze.
implementation: Declare the sun direction once (elevation 6 deg, azimuth 250 deg) and drive the key, the rim and any painted-in shading from that single value.
Set the fill as a HemisphereLight with a cool sky and a warm-dark ground so undersides pick up bounce colour instead of going neutral.
Add the rim as a second weak DirectionalLight roughly opposite the key with castShadow false; it separates silhouettes from the sky without creating a competing shadow set.
Fit the shadow camera to the visible scene extent (20 m here); an oversized extent wastes the 2048 map and produces the stair-stepping usually blamed on bias.
Use normalBias 0.03 to remove shadow acne on curved surfaces before reaching for a larger negative bias, which detaches contact shadows.
Keep exposure at 0.9 and tune the key intensity against it; raising exposure to brighten the shade will clip the sky.
observable_checks: Shadows on a common flat receiver run parallel and are at least three times the caster height, confirming the stated elevation.
A grayscale screenshot still separates lit from shaded planes, confirming the read does not depend on colour alone.
The shaded side of a neutral object samples as cool and non-zero, confirming the sky fill is present.
Turning fog off changes distance separation but leaves foreground exposure unchanged.

creative_affordances: Sky and sun colours can be pushed well past anything a real sunset produces; the requirement is that all shadows still agree with the one declared direction.
The rim can be recoloured to an invented source, a second sun or a city glow, as long as it stays below the key.
known_limits: Every number in this profile was tuned for ACESFilmic tone mapping at exposure 0.9; under a different tone-mapping curve or exposure the intensities and fog density must be re-derived, not copied.
No renderer run for this record; values are authored starting points.

defaults.rationale: Low warm key with a cool sky fill gives the long-shadow, rim-lit read of golden hour; fog matches the horizon band; exposure below 1 keeps the sun disc from clipping while the key at 3.2 still lifts the lit planes well clear of the fill. Kelvin-to-hex conversions here are authored approximations, not colorimetric transforms (2700K~#ffb46b, 3200K~#ffc58f, 4500K~#ffe4c4, 5600K~#fff4e5, 6500K~#ffffff, open shade 8000K~#cfe0ff).

values.time_of_day: 20 min before sunset, sun elevation 6 deg
values.intensity_unit: three-intensity (lux-scaled for Directional/Hemisphere, candela for Point/Spot; tuned with the stated tone_mapping.exposure)
never: shadows that disagree with the declared azimuth
